2.body: The core concern (from the article's lede): "There is growing concern that AI can blunt memory and reasoning. But science shows ways to keep the brain sharp."
2.breadcrumbs: AI and the Cognitive-Decline Concern » AI and the Cognitive-Decline Concern
2.title: AI and the Cognitive-Decline Concern

3.body: Lixiang Yan (education researcher) realized students could outsource all of their work for his university course to AI — the concrete case that frames the article. This fits the pattern of related coverage: universities embracing AI while asking whether "students get smarter or stop thinking."
3.breadcrumbs: AI and the Cognitive-Decline Concern » The triggering case
3.title: The triggering case

4.body: AI-assisted work shifts cognitive labor from the human to the model: recall, retrieval, and reasoning practice are the very exercises that keep memory and reasoning sharp. The concern is not that AI is "bad," but that unexamined reliance reduces the mental effort that maintains cognitive skills. The article's counterpoint: the science of critical thinking offers ways to keep the brain sharp even in an AI-heavy workflow. Related: The Science of Critical Thinking · The Nine Cited Studies · Full text (available parts)
4.breadcrumbs: AI and the Cognitive-Decline Concern » Why it matters
4.title: Why it matters

5.body: The article's second half argues that science shows ways to keep the brain sharp in the age of AI — i.e., critical thinking is a trainable, measurable skill, not a fixed trait.
5.breadcrumbs: The Science of Critical Thinking » The Science of Critical Thinking
5.title: The Science of Critical Thinking

6.body: Cognitive training works: the 2002 Cognitive Instruction study (Remy, Schmidt & Boshuizen) on instructional design for cognitive skills is the oldest citation — evidence that structured practice improves thinking. AI changes the task landscape: Bastani et al. ( PNAS 2025) and Yan et al. ( Nature Reviews Psychology 2025) situate AI's impact on how people learn and think. Measuring the effect: Chesire et al. ( Trials 2024) — an RCT-style study on AI-assisted learning; Kops et al. ( Computers in Human Behavior 2025); Mendoza et al. ( Media Asia 2024); Axelsson et al. ( Journal of Research in Technology in Education 2023) — AI tools in education and their effects. The mechanism: McGrew ( Current Opinion in Psychology 2024) and Eliseev & Marsh ( Applied Cognitive Psychology 2023) address how offloading to AI (e.g., memory tasks) changes learning.
6.breadcrumbs: The Science of Critical Thinking » What the cited literature supports
6.title: What the cited literature supports

7.body: Keep deliberate practice in the loop: retrieval practice, source evaluation, and argument construction are the "workouts" for memory and reasoning. Use AI as a sparring partner (generating counterarguments, asking "why") rather than as a substitute for doing the thinking yourself. The reference list is the research base behind this position — see The Nine Cited Studies . Related: AI and the Cognitive-Decline Concern · Full text (available parts)

9.body: The Nature article page links four sibling articles framing the debate: In praise of human teachers: universities must resist outsourcing everything to AI — the institutional response: keep human instruction in the loop. Is AI ruining our skills? Early results are in — and they're not good — early empirical results on skill atrophy. Universities are embracing AI: will students get smarter or stop thinking? — the central open question of the AI-in-education debate. Are the Internet and AI affecting our memory? What the science says — evidence on the "Google effect" (cognitive offloading to external storage). These frame Pearson's piece within Nature's broader coverage: AI adoption in universities + measurable cognitive costs + the science of counteracting them. Related: AI and the Cognitive-Decline Concern · Full text (available parts)
